quiz2.q: You set the temperature to zero in the settings and sent the exact same prompt three times in a row. What will you most likely see?
options: Three noticeably different answers: randomness is built into the network itself and doesn't depend on temperature
Three (almost) identical answers: the roulette wheel turns into greedy decoding, and the leading token wins at every step
The model will refuse to answer: at zero temperature the probabilities can't be computed
The answers will become longer and more detailed: low temperature makes the model try harder
quiz2.explain: At a temperature near zero, the distribution sharpens to the limit: the leader takes practically everything, and sampling collapses into greedy decoding. All the randomness lived in the wheel, not inside the network — take it away, and the answers coincide.

quiz2.q: At what point in the pipeline — from your prompt to the finished answer — does randomness enter the game?
options: In the attention mechanism: the network's layers fire slightly differently each time
When the text is sliced into tokens: the slicing comes out different every time
In softmax: it divides the percentages among the tokens at random
Only at the very last step, when the roulette wheel picks one token from the ready-made probabilities
quiz2.explain: The entire network computes deterministically right up to the output: the same input — the same logits and the same percentages after softmax. Randomness appears only at the sampling step, when the wheel picks one token from the distribution.

quiz2.q: The model is running at a high temperature, but top-p = 0.9 is switched on. The token "democracy" from the module's example had a microscopic probability. What happens to it at this step?
options: It won't make it into the wheel at all: the top of the list will accumulate its 90% without it, and the tail gets discarded
Its chances will grow: high temperature boosts precisely the rare tokens
It will take part in the lottery with its tiny chance — top-p excludes no one
Top-p will force-pick it, to make the text more varied
quiz2.explain: Top-p sorts tokens by descending probability and keeps only the top that together accumulates 90%; the deep tail sits out the lottery. That's exactly how it insures against wild tokens whose chances crept up because of the high temperature.

quiz2.q: A chatbot has typed half a sentence and keeps writing. At that moment, what can be said about how the sentence will end?
options: It has already been computed in full and is simply displayed with a delay, for effect
It exists as a draft that the model keeps polishing as it types
It doesn't exist yet: each next token will be chosen anew, in light of everything already written
It was chosen the moment the model read your question
quiz2.explain: Autoregression means there is no finished plan for the sentence: the chosen token is appended to the text, and the probabilities of the next one are recomputed from scratch. Word-by-word typing isn't an animation — it's the real pace at which the answer is born.

quiz2.q: Why does the request "reason step by step" genuinely help the model, if you recall the mechanism of autoregression?
options: The intermediate reasoning gets appended to the context and influences the probabilities of all subsequent tokens
That phrase automatically lowers the temperature to a safe level
The model switches to a separate "logic" block that otherwise stays off
The model gains the ability to check and rewrite the text it has already printed
quiz2.explain: The model can't "think it through to the end first, then write it down": whatever's been chosen is already in the text. But intermediate steps, once in the context, shift the probabilities of the tokens that follow — reasoning out loud literally paves the road to the answer.

quiz2.q: How does a modern LLM's generation loop differ from the Markov chain at the start of the course?
options: An LLM picks words with no randomness at all, while a Markov chain picks at random
A Markov chain works with letters, while an LLM works with whole sentences at once
The loop itself — "predict — append — repeat" — is the same; what differs is the predictor: instead of a little table of word pairs, a huge attention-equipped network
In every way: an LLM first builds a complete plan of the answer and then writes it down
quiz2.explain: The principle hasn't changed one iota: pick a token, append it, predict onward. The difference is in who produces the probabilities — for a Markov chain it's a table of word pairs; for an LLM, a network with dozens of attention layers, trained on enormous texts.

exercises.q: Explain in your own words what people mean when they say: "a language model doesn't output the next word — it outputs a forecast." What exactly comes out of the network, and how does a word eventually come out of that?
exercises.ref: What comes out of the network isn't a word but a score for every token in the vocabulary: raw logits, which softmax turns into probabilities — something like a weather forecast ("rug" — 54%, "windowsill" — 24%). The word itself appears in a separate step: the roulette wheel picks a token at random, in proportion to those percentages. And temperature and top-p are settings of that wheel, not of the network itself.

exercises.q: Predict what happens: you ask the model to write a short formal letter to the tax office, but the temperature is accidentally set to 1.8. What will the text be like, and which setting would you change?
exercises.ref: At a temperature of 1.8, the distribution flattens out: the wheel's sectors even out, and unexpected underdog words break into the text more and more often. The formal letter will most likely come out odd — with sudden turns of phrase and, in places, outright nonsense. The fix is lowering the temperature (say, to 0.2–0.3): formal and factual texts need predictability, not daring.

exercises.q: Give your own example of a real-life process built like autoregression: the next step is chosen in light of everything already done, and there's no complete plan in advance. Explain what plays the role of the "appended token" in your example.
exercises.ref: An improvised spoken story works well, for example: there's no prepared script, each next sentence is born from what's already been said, and one unexpected remark steers the whole story down a different road. The role of the "appended token" is played by the sentence you've just spoken: it becomes part of the context and shapes what you say next. The essence of any such example: each step's result becomes the next step's input, and a complete plan never exists in advance.
